item.title: Windows kept resetting my default apps until I changed one policy setting for good
item.itunes:title: Windows kept resetting my default apps until I changed one policy setting for good
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Windows 11 is quite unusual, in that it has a rather funny habit of forgetting what you've already told it. I have Google Chrome set as my default browser, and yet, occasionally, I'll double-click an HTML document only to watch Windows open it on Microsoft Edge instead. It's particularly vexing because Edge is one of those Windows components I can't get rid of, despite having absolutely zero use for it.

This isn't because I haven't set my default correctly. Windows has several mechanisms for managing file associations, and on PCs managed through a domain, administrators can even enforce those associations through Group Policy. It's quite interesting because I've found this one approach to be amongst the ones that sticks and doesn't need you to revisit your default apps as often as I do.

Windows 11 doesn't always respect your default app

Setting a default browser isn't always a one-click fix to the woes

Windows 11 gives you a number of ways to designate which app you want to use for a particular file type or extension. If you set Chrome, Brave, or Firefox as your default web browser, you'd expect, like any reasonable user, for all webpages and HTML file to follow suit. As such, it's mighty disappointing when they don't.

I ran into this particular issue with .htm and .html file types more often than I could recall. Chrome was evidently my default browser, and that much was clear from the constant nudges Edge gave me to set it as my default every time I'd accidentally launch it. Yet, double-clicking an HTML document could still send it straight to Edge. Windows simply isn't very good at respecting user-defined parameters, and the constant updates can sometimes make it even more convoluted.

It isn't just a problem that's specific to my machine, if you were skeptical. At any given point of time, you can expect a live thread on Microsoft's Tech Community forums from someone wondering why Windows has once again decided that their chosen defaults feel like nothing more than a suggestion. As a matter of fact, the latest thread about a user complaining that Windows' monthly updates repeatedly kept resetting their preferred browser, PDF reader, and video player went live 4 days prior to the time of writing. Clearly, it's an ongoing issue.

You can enforce your default apps through Group Policy

With a few minutes, and a few edits to the XML file

Fortunately, there's an approach that takes care of the changing default apps problem. For this, you will require an XML file that instructs Windows which applications should handle a particular file type or a protocol. Windows 11 can create most of this for you with a few steps.

The first thing you would want to do is open Windows PowerShell or Command Prompt with elevated permissions (this means right-clicking and running as an administrator). Then, you want to export your current default associations with the following command.

Dism /Online /Export-DefaultAppAssociations:C:\DefaultAssoc.xml 

Once that is done, DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) will report that as completed successfully, and you'll have obtained an XML file at C:\DefaultAssoc.xml containing your current file association. This will be useful later.

Now, you want to open the XML in a Notepad. I just used the following PowerShell command.

notepad C:\DefaultAssoc.xml

You'll notice that it's a long, scary file. There is no reason to be concerned. Windows simply gives you association for a huge number of file types on your PC.

Now, the next step is to just edit the associations you want to change. In my case, I just wanted Chrome to handle my HTML files, so I looked for the existing entries for .htm and .html and changed them to the following.

<Association Identifier=".htm" ProgId="ChromeHTML" ApplicationName="Google Chrome"/>
<Association Identifier=".html" ProgId="ChromeHTML" ApplicationName="Google Chrome"/>

Next, you'd want to save the XML file, but also make sure Notepad doesn't make it into a .txt. If you're using "Save As", it's worth making sure you select "All files" and retain the .xml extension.

Manage files without clutter

4
By  Sumukh Rao

Tell Windows to use your new association file

The Group Policy setting is where the changes are reflected

When the XML is saved, you need to instruct Windows to use it. This is done via the Local Group Policy Editor for individual machines, although domain admins can apply it through Group Policy Management.

To get started quickly, you need to hold Windows + R and type gpedit.msc in the dialogue box. Pressing Enter will take you to the Local Group Policy Editor.

You have to head into Computer Configuration, followed by Administrative Templates, then Windows Components, and then File Explorer. Here, you're looking for a policy called Set a default file associations configuration file. Double click, set it to Enabled, and then enter the location of your XML file under Default Associations Configuration File. If you followed the steps so far exactly the same way, it'll be on the C: drive, in which case you need to set it to C:\DefaultAssoc.xml. Click Apply, and then OK.

Now, all you need to do is restart your PC and sign back in. This should reflect the changes to the default apps as applied on your XML file.

Bonus Approach: Use SetUserFTA

Because it always helps to know there's an easier alternative

If you've gone through the trouble of exporting and editing an XML and found the Group Policy method to be either a hassle or just too complicated, you're not alone. Additionally, if you're on a personal machine that isn't a part of a managed network, Windows will acknowledge the policy but still ignore it. Fret not, though, because there's a simple, free tool that can get you the same results without the pain involved in the process.

SetUserFTA by Christoph Kolbicz offers this alternative. It's a free command-line utility that writes file associations directly to the registry that bypasses the UserChoiceProtection Driver. You can download the SetUserFTA tool from the official website, extract it, and open a CMD or PowerShell in the same folder, and then edit the associations like so.

.\SetUserFTA.exe .html ChromeHTML
.\SetUserFTA.exe .htm ChromeHTML
I fixed Windows 11 File Explorer lag by disabling this legacy service

A quarter-century old service we no longer need.

13
By  Samarveer Singh

Windows doesn't always remember your choices, but you can make it so it does

It's tiresome to constantly remind Windows 11 about your preferences surrounding default apps, but until Microsoft makes these default associations less temperamental (or better, stops breaking them with every third update), Group Policy and SetUserFTA offer a convenient way to make your preferences stick.

item.title: Disabling this router setting feels like a quick fix for lag, but it's actually keeping your busy network alive
item.itunes:title: Disabling this router setting feels like a quick fix for lag, but it's actually keeping your busy network alive
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It seems we're always "fixing" our Wi-Fi connections without ever getting there. Wireless networks have to deal with interference, latency, congestion, jitter, and a host of other things, and this keeps users on their toes. On one of these Wi-Fi fixing adventures, you may have come across "OFDMA" in your router's settings, and disabling it may even have improved your connection for a while.

OFDMA is a Wi-Fi 6 feature that is intended to keep your Wi-Fi snappy even when multiple devices are vying for high-speed links to the router. You should leave it enabled in most situations to ensure your latency-sensitive devices aren't waiting around.

Your 5-year-old router isn't just slow — it's an unpatched security loophole

Don't risk everything with an outdated router

By  Tanveer Singh

OFDMA is a core Wi-Fi 6 feature designed to minimize latency

There's a reason it's enabled

Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access, or OFDMA, is an improvement over Wi-Fi 5's OFDM. The latter allowed only a single device to use a particular wireless channel at a time, with every other device waiting for their turn. This arrangement works fine when you only have a handful of devices, but falls apart in the presence of an extensive home network.

OFDMA allows your router to divide a wireless channel into smaller resource units (RUs), which it can assign to multiple devices. This enables more than one device to access the same transmission window simultaneously instead of waiting in a single file. So, your smartphone browsing Instagram, laptop running a video call, and a smart bulb sending a status ping can transmit at the same time.

On the uplink side, OFDMA allows your devices to send synchronized data packets to the router in a single window. This makes OFDMA one of the core Wi-Fi 6 features that prevents your home network from feeling sluggish.

Wi-Fi 7 routers are finally here, but most homes aren't wired well enough to take advantage

Your home is probably not ready for Wi-Fi 7, and won't be for a long time

13
By  Tanveer Singh

Diagnosing laggy Wi-Fi can make you disable OFDMA

But it's crucial for most modern wireless networks

It's possible that your Wi-Fi feels better after disabling OFDMA, or the "AX" setting in the router settings, but the improvement is often a false positive. An older device on a modern Wi-Fi 6 network might be dealing with an unrelated issue, such as a security handshake mismatch or band-steering incompatibility. Turning off Wi-Fi 6 altogether (since many routers don't expose an isolated OFDMA setting), can seemingly make the connection faster.

This is because a few devices on an uncontested network will not show any difference between OFDMA on and off. An isolated speed test may show the same (or better) performance after disabling OFDMA, but this doesn't mean anything. If you perform a better test by running simultaneous traffic on modern devices, such as a laptop, PC, smartphone, and smart TV, you'll most likely find that OFDMA enabled is the preferred scenario.

Instead of trying to disable core Wi-Fi features like OFDMA, inspect physical interference, co-channel interference, channel width settings, and the presence of slower legacy devices on your Wi-Fi network.

I finally made my Wi-Fi snappier by changing the most ignored setting on my router

Your router's transmit power isn't supposed to be at the maximum level

11
By  Tanveer Singh

Disabling Wi-Fi features can be tempting, but you should proceed with caution

When you're dealing with a laggy connection and nothing seems to fix it, you may be inclined to use drastic measures. However, disabling foundational Wi-Fi features like OFDMA will often have the opposite effect. OFDMA is key to supporting multiple devices on your Wi-Fi, and disabling it is unlikely to fix your Wi-Fi lag.

item.title: The free video editor I use instead of Premiere hasn't asked me for a subscription in five years
item.itunes:title: The free video editor I use instead of Premiere hasn't asked me for a subscription in five years
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Whenever you leave flagship software, it usually comes with a catch, and a general sense that you gave something up. That's the position I'm still in after canceling my After Effects subscription. But Premiere Pro is a different story because it's easier to find free NLEs than VFX editors.

Plenty of the alternatives have been through my setup over the years. Shotcut, OpenShot, Pikimov, Natron, and even Blender have all come and gone. But one of them lasted longer than the others, and it's actually the first open-source Premiere alternative I laid my hands on…

This open-source tool combines Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and After Effects - And it replaced all three for me

I didn't expect it to replace my entire Adobe setup

13
By  Nolen Jonker

Why Kdenlive outlasted every other Premiere alternative I tried

It isn't only about the price tag

The simplest reason it's still here is that it's the Premiere alternative I've reached for the longest, so it has longevity going for it over the others. Tools that don't catch my attention quickly become forgotten on my computer, but I still have Kdenlive pinned to my taskbar. The non-existent price tag is the headline, obviously.

Not only is it free to use, but it has absolutely zero paid tiers preventing you from using more advanced features. Kdenlive is also open-source, made by the KDE community rather than a company that needs to answer to shareholders, so there's nobody who's in a position to hike the price or shut it down for whatever reason.

But most other Premiere alternatives share this same philosophy, so why Kdenlive? I'd say the format is something that rarely comes up, but one that matters the most. item.title: The Gemini app for Windows lets you bring up your fave AI with a simple hotkey
item.itunes:title: The Gemini app for Windows lets you bring up your fave AI with a simple hotkey
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • The Gemini app for Windows is now generally available as a desktop app with full features.
  • Invoke Gemini instantly anywhere with the Alt+Space hotkey—no browser switch needed.
  • Includes Gemini Spark, Drive integration, Nano Banana image gen, and Gemini Omni video tools.

If you're a big fan of Gemini, you may not enjoy the part where you have to boot up your browser every time you want to ask it a question. Fortunately, Google knows this and has released a new Gemini app for Windows to make it easier for people to access their LLM. The best part is, the app comes with a hotkey that lets you quickly invoke Gemini, no matter what's on your screen at that time.

Google's Gemini app for Windows brings its popular LLM to the desktop

Two keypresses and you're there

Credit: Google

As announced on the Google Blog, the company has announced the general release of its Windows client. From the press release, it looks like you're getting the full experience without any cut features; the company specifically names Gemini Spark, Google Drive integration, Nano Banana image generation, and Gemini Omni video creation in the post.

The real benefit of the desktop app is how easy it is to access Gemini when you need it most:

"Press Alt + Space on your PC at any time to open Gemini over your active work. Whether you need a quick fact-check on a document or a few catchy title ideas for a presentation, you can get the help you need and jump right back into your workflow."

It seems very useful when you're working away and you want to bring up Gemini to answer a question or solve a query without navigating away from your current page; definitely a huge plus for the Gemini power-users out there.

If you'd like to give the Gemini app for Windows a shot, head over to the download page and grab it starting right now.

I tried Gemini Omni, and it's so good it feels straight out of science fiction

There's a new king of video generation in town, and it's no joke

3
By  Abhinav Raj

item.title: OpenAI reveals its new Data agent for ChatGPT Work to make your job a lot easier
item.itunes:title: OpenAI reveals its new Data agent for ChatGPT Work to make your job a lot easier
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • OpenAI launched a Data agent for ChatGPT Work; use @data to analyze your datasets.
  • It connects to Redshift, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, MongoDB, Datadog, ClickHouse and files.
  • Ask questions or request graphs to find trends, anomalies, and shareable summaries; no copy-pasting needed.

Collecting data is one thing; making it all make sense is another. Fortunately, OpenAI has released a new agent to help you with the last part. The company has announced a new Data agent for ChatGPT Work; all you need to do is feed it your data, ask it a question, and let it do all the heavy lifting.

ChatGPT Work's Data agent makes sense of trends and anomalies in your data

No more sifting through information yourself

Credit: OpenAI

As announced on the OpenAI website, the ChatGPT Work plugin now has access to a data agent. To use it, make sure you have access to ChatGPT Work (it requires a ChatGPT Plus sub aet the very least), then enable the Data plugin. Once both are ready to roll, go to the website or app, make sure you're in ChatGPT Work mode, then type @data into your prompt window to get started.

Now you can ask ChatGPT a question about your data; perhaps something went wrong, and you're not sure why, or maybe you're on the hunt for trends. Similarly, you can tell the LLM to sum up your data into handy graphs to present to people in an easy-to-digest fashion.

The best bit is, you don't need to copy-paste your books over to ChatGPT Work:

The Data agent connects to approved data sources including Amazon Redshift, Datadog, Google BigQuery, ClickHouse, Databricks, MongoDB, Snowflake, and more. It can also bring files and documents from Google Drive and SharePoint into the analysis.

Everything you need to get analyzing should already be live on your account, so give it a try and see if ChatGPT can sift through your data and reach conclusions you hadn't thought of.

I stopped paying for ChatGPT after putting my local LLM on Tailscale

My phone finally reaches my home server the same way it reaches ChatGPT.

item.title: I tested Nvidia's leaked DLSS 5 build on my RTX 40-series across 3 games, and it changed what I thought about neural rendering
item.itunes:title: I tested Nvidia's leaked DLSS 5 build on my RTX 40-series across 3 games, and it changed what I thought about neural rendering
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A lot has been said about Nvidia's highly contentious DLSS 5, but very little has actually been seen, and even less has been benchmarked. After all, DLSS 5 was never originally supposed to come to my RTX 4070 Ti Super. And yet, it seems like it has arrived all the same, thanks to the efforts of the modding community. That got me thinking about what Team Green's latest generation of GeForce cards is really selling.

My tests with a leaked build of Nvidia's latest release left me asking whether DLSS 5 could be worth using at all, even on hardware it's purpose-built for. Just how much of a case does neural rendering actually make for upgrading? The easiest way to find out was to put the build through three of my most beloved titles and see what Blackwell's latest party trick is, and if that's something my experience with gaming on Ada Lovelace is missing.

The utility used in the following tests to run DLSS 5 Neural Rendering was rakanki911's DLSS 5 Swapper version 2.2.3, which is a community DLL-swapper that installs the leaked DLSS 5 files alongside RenoDX as well as ReShade. Accordingly, the results should be construed as indicative only as this configuration relies on a pre-release, unofficial build deployed through a third-party injection layer.

Grand Theft Auto V Enhanced

It came out on the Xbox 360 and PS3, and now it's here

GTA V is more than a decade old. It launched in the year 2013 on the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3. Two years later, it graced the PC in 2015, which was when most high-end builds were running the GTX 980 Ti, the fastest CPU you could get was the Intel Core i7-6700K, and RAM was... well, affordable.

By all standards of measure, it's an ancient title in 2026, and yet, there's something almost miraculous that a variant of DLSS 5 does with it that makes you want to experience the streets of Los Santos all over again. There's an undeniable improvement to visual depth in the atmosphere, NPCs, and characters, a grounded sense of realism in weather effects (in this case, rain) and reflective surfaces. It is, however, the city in motion that truly sells it.

Just like every other game that appears on this list, I tested GTA V on the same hardware consisting of my RTX 4070 Ti Super paired with a Ryzen 5 7600X and 32GB of DDR5-6000 at 1440p, with each title running its maximum graphics preset with ray tracing enabled. Frame generation and Smooth Motion were disabled to isolate the performance cost of the neural rendering pipeline.

In performance, it is worth noting that all three NR presets landed well within 2 FPS of each other, suggesting that the preset has more bearing on visuals than on performance. It can be reasonably expected to experience a 36–38% average FPS cost and a further 31–36% hit on 1% lows regardless of which model is picked.

A lot has been said about Nvidia's highly contentious DLSS 5, but very little has actually been seen, and even less has been benchmarked. After all, DLSS 5 was never originally supposed to come to my RTX 4070 Ti Super. And yet, it seems like it has arrived all the same, thanks to the efforts of the modding community. That got me thinking about what Team Green's latest generation of GeForce cards is really selling.

My tests with a leaked build of Nvidia's latest release left me asking whether DLSS 5 could be worth using at all, even on hardware it's purpose-built for. Just how much of a case does neural rendering actually make for upgrading? The easiest way to find out was to put the build through three of my most beloved titles and see what Blackwell's latest party trick is, and if that's something my experience with gaming on Ada Lovelace is missing.

The utility used in the following tests to run DLSS 5 Neural Rendering was rakanki911's DLSS 5 Swapper version 2.2.3, which is a community DLL-swapper that installs the leaked DLSS 5 files alongside RenoDX as well as ReShade. By all standards of measure, it's an ancient title in 2026, and yet, there's something almost miraculous that a variant of DLSS 5 does with it that makes you want to experience the streets of Los Santos all over again. There's an undeniable improvement to visual depth in the atmosphere, NPCs, and characters, a grounded sense of realism in weather effects (in this case, rain) and reflective surfaces. It is, however, the city in motion that truly sells it.

item.title: I totally transformed Jellyfin’s video player with one simple plugin
item.itunes:title: I totally transformed Jellyfin’s video player with one simple plugin
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The coolest thing about self-hosting media with Jellyfin is the community of developers who make it even better with plugins and alternative clients. For instance, the Jellyfin Cinema Project plugin turns my library into a 3D theater. I recently discovered another great plugin that improves the video player experience, and it is from the same developer as Cinema Project.

VideoOSD Tweaks & Candy changes how I navigate videos while watching on Jellyfin Web. It improves the on-screen display (OSD) controls and artwork I want by adding functionality not native to the Jellyfin video experience, such as playback speed steps, frame-by-frame navigation, episode chapter artwork, and much more.

VideoOSD Tweaks & Candy plugin

A better Jellyfin video experience

The VideoOSD Tweaks & Candy plugin for Jellyfin isn't a separate player, client, skin, or theme. It's also not an individual Jellyfin app. It's a plugin that integrates directly with my Jellyfin server and adds new ways to control video playback on the web. Before you install the OSD plugin, install the File Transformation plugin first, then restart your server. Once that's running, install the VideoOSD Tweaks & Candy plugin and restart the server.

Go into the Plugins section, find the plugin, and open Settings to configure it. You can make several changes here. I started by adding everything in the Add-on section under the General header. You can add buttons for screenshots, downloads, framestep, and more that aren't included in standard Jellyfin web media playback. In addition to what you can add, another highlight is what you can hide.

For instance, I can take away all the standard Jellyfin web player buttons, including play/pause, casting, syncplay, the volume slider, and more. I can show only the custom VideoOSD Tweaks and Candy buttons, none of the Jellyfin controls, or a mix of both. So far, having a mix seems to work best for my playback experience.

The available settings allow me to tweak the controls exactly how I want them. To get the Jellyfin web OSD controls to really shine, you have to dig through the settings and do a lot of trial and error. It might sound frustrating, but if you like several customization options for your player, you will have a fun time doing it.

Not only can I choose the buttons, but I can select where they are placed on the screen, which is divided into four sections. I can also change the order in which each button appears. Plus, with the Candy settings, I can configure artwork on the display while watching a movie or show. It really provides a more immersive experience than Jellyfin.

4 free Jellyfin tools that make my media server feel like a premium streaming service

I've caught the automation bug, I'm afraid

2
By  Samarveer Singh

VideoOSD Tweaks & Candy limitations

Fix browser cache if controls aren't there

I must admit, I had a difficult time getting this working correctly at first. I installed it according to the instructions on the GitHub page and ran it in Chrome, using server version 10.11.11. That allowed me to hide Jellyfin's playback buttons, but the custom controls and candy effects wouldn't display. Sometimes the buttons I set to hide wouldn't, which was also frustrating.

However, there is a practical workaround. Load the plugin's settings and choose what you want, right-click the screen, choose Inspect > Network, and check the Disable cache box. Hit Ctrl+R to refresh the page and go back and play a video. This worked each time I added a new button or made other configuration changes.

Button configurations not showing up right away isn't the plugin's fault. It's because of how web browser caching works. A browser holds on to an old cached copy of the page or script instead of loading new settings. So, disabling the cache and reloading the page clears everything, allowing the new buttons or artwork to display.

I tried it in multiple browsers with Jellyfin versions 10.10.7 and 10.11.11 and was successful using the browser workaround. I tried the plugin on Jellyfin version 12.0 RC5, but had no luck getting it to work there. Of course, the developer notes that it was built and tested on version 10.10.7 and Google Chrome, and all Chromium-based browsers worked for me. Firefox was a bit more picky about handling the plugin. Once the controls load, playback is similar to standalone players like VLC or MPV.

A refreshing Jellyfin video player plugin

Freedom of playback

When you get your Jellyfin server up and running and play your first video from the web player, the playback controls you see are all that are provided. You must settle for what Jellyfin gives you. There are only a limited number of player customization options available. This plugin changes that by adding more controls and overlay artwork while you play a video.

You can add video logos, clear art, banners, backdrops, and more. Another cool ability is displaying individual season art for shows if you have it in your media library. So, in addition to the customization available in the playback controls, there are plenty of tweaks you can make to get the visuals to look the way you want.

A better web player for Jellyfin content on the web

Overall, I have had a blast with this plugin, and it has changed the way I watch videos from a browser on Jellyfin. Like Cinema Project, I would love to see it come to more platforms. There are a ton of customizations, and it's nice to have more choice than standard Jellyfin playback buttons. I can hide all Jellyfin OSD controls and only use VideoOSD controls, or combine the two. The added artwork settings improve the web player experience.

This open-source media player finally unified my Jellyfin library and YouTube into one interface

Fathom combines Jellyfin, YouTube and media requests into a single player — and it's a game changer for cord-cutters

item.itunes:summary:
I didn’t get into 3D printing because I had a long list of household problems waiting for custom plastic parts. I wanted to print an articulated dragon. That was it, and I seriously underestimated how much I’d have to learn before I could get one off the build plate the way I wanted. Weeks later, after dealing with first layers, adhesion, orientation, supports, slicer settings, and failed attempts, I finally had the dragon. By then, it had already taught me how to approach nearly everything else I wanted to print.

9 alternatives to Benchy for calibrating your 3D printer

For calibrating your 3D printer, Benchy isn't the only game in town. Here are other 3D test models you can use to dial in your 3D printer.

By  Jeff Butts

Having one specific goal made learning much easier

I always knew exactly what success needed to look like

Having one specific thing I wanted to make turned out to be much more useful than simply deciding I wanted to “learn 3D printing.” I wasn’t downloading random models to see whether the printer could make them. Every attempt shared the same goal, so when something changed from one print to the next, I could focus on what had improved. More importantly, I cared whether the thing worked.

The easiest possible print isn’t automatically the best one if you have no interest in the result.

An articulated dragon isn’t the simplest model to start with, as I learned pretty quickly. It has a lot going on compared with a solid decorative object, and all those sections need to come off the printer cleanly yet remain movable. A flaw I might have shrugged off on something simpler became obvious when one section of the dragon didn’t behave as it should. That made it hard to convince myself that a merely passable print was good enough.

It also gave the terminology I was learning some context. First-layer problems weren’t just something people on forums warned beginners about because I could see what happened when that part of the print wasn’t right. Orientation stopped being an abstract slicer decision when I had a model in front of me that depended on how the printer built it. I wasn’t memorizing a bunch of 3D printing rules. I was trying to get the dragon to work.

Failed dragon prints became useful troubleshooting exercises

Each bad print gave me another problem to diagnose

At first, it was tempting to treat a failed print as the printer doing something weird. That’s a convenient explanation when you’re still staring at slicer options you barely understand. After enough attempts at the same model, though, I couldn’t keep doing that. I had to start looking at what had actually changed and which part of the print was telling me something had gone wrong.

Using the same model over and over helped more than I expected. If I changed something and the next dragon printed better, there was at least a reason to suspect that adjustment had helped. If it got worse, I could go back and rethink it rather than wonder whether I’d just picked a more difficult model this time. It wasn’t a perfect experiment, but it was much more useful than jumping from one random download to another.

I also learned quickly that changing everything at once is a terrible way to figure out anything. If I adjusted several things and the print suddenly improved, I still didn’t know which change had made the difference. That habit of isolating problems stayed with me long after the dragon was finished. Now I’m much more inclined to look at the failure, decide what I think caused it, and make one sensible adjustment instead of throwing settings at the problem until something works.

The dragon taught lessons that applied everywhere else

My later projects benefited from mistakes I made early

Somewhere along the way, the dragon stopped being the only point of the exercise. I still wanted a successful one, obviously, but I noticed the same lessons kept showing up in completely different prints. Bed adhesion wasn’t just the annoying thing preventing this particular model from finishing. It was something I needed to pay attention to whenever a new project depended on a good first layer.

The same was true for how I looked at models before printing them. I became less willing to load something into the slicer and immediately send it to the printer without thinking about what would actually happen once the first layer went down. Orientation mattered. Small contact areas mattered. The model itself mattered, and I started looking at those things before committing hours to a print, rather than afterward, when there was already failed plastic on the build plate.

When a print fails, avoid changing several settings at once. Pick the most likely cause, change one thing, and try again. Keeping the model the same makes it much easier to tell whether that adjustment actually helped.

I also stopped assuming that a successful print meant I’d done everything correctly. Some models are more forgiving than others, and that can hide mediocre decisions pretty well. The dragon didn’t let me get away with that as easily because there were more places for a small problem to become visible. Once I’d worked through those problems, simpler prints became easier to evaluate because I had a better idea of what I was actually looking for.

Starting with something easier would have been sensible

A calibration model probably would have caused less frustration

There’s a perfectly good argument that I made this harder on myself than it needed to be. An articulated dragon isn’t exactly the obvious beginner project if your main goal is to learn efficiently. Calibration models exist for a reason, and simpler objects can isolate one problem at a time without requiring you to juggle several variables. I probably could’ve learned some of the same lessons with far fewer failed prints.

That would’ve been less frustrating, too. When you’re still learning which settings actually affect print quality, a complicated failure can point you in several directions at once. You can spend time worrying about adhesion when the issue is elsewhere, or start changing slicer settings that were perfectly fine to begin with. I did enough second-guessing while learning without needing a model that made diagnosis any easier to get wrong.

There’s nothing especially noble about choosing the harder route, either. Starting with straightforward prints gives you a chance to understand the machine before adding more demanding models to the mix. If someone asked me for the most efficient beginner curriculum, I wouldn’t hand them an articulated dragon and tell them to keep printing it until everything made sense. There are much cleaner ways to learn.

Wanting the finished print kept me working through failures

Efficiency mattered less because I actually wanted this result

The problem is that I’m not sure I would’ve cared enough about the cleaner route. A calibration cube might have taught me something useful, but I didn’t get interested in 3D printing because I desperately wanted a shelf full of calibration objects. I wanted the dragon. Every annoying failed attempt still had a reason behind it because there was an actual result I wanted on the other side.

That made a difference when I started getting tired of trying again. It’s easy to abandon a practice print because nothing meaningful changes if you never finish it. Walking away from the dragon meant I still didn’t have the thing that had pushed me toward 3D printing in the first place. So I’d look at what went wrong, make another adjustment, and try again, even when I was getting pretty tired of seeing the same model in the slicer.

That experience changed what I consider a good beginner project. The easiest possible print isn’t automatically the best if you have no interest in the result. Something a little beyond your current ability can give you a reason to learn what the printer is actually doing instead of just following instructions until a test model succeeds. In my case, that motivation happened to be an articulated dragon, and being stubborn about finishing it proved useful.

One successful dragon ended up teaching much more

By the time I finally had the articulated dragon I’d been trying to make, getting the model itself was almost the smaller payoff. I’d learned to watch the first layers more carefully, think about how a model would print before starting, and diagnose failures rather than immediately rerunning the same job. I’d also learned not to panic and change five settings just because something looked wrong. All of that carried over into the projects I printed afterward.

I could’ve worked through tutorials and calibration models in a sensible order and probably learned the fundamentals faster. Instead, I spent weeks repeatedly trying to print one thing I genuinely wanted, and I learned those fundamentals because I needed them to finish it. The dragon eventually became another successful print in a growing collection. The useful part was everything I had to figure out before I could make it successfully.

item.itunes:title: My spreadsheet workflow changed when I ditched Excel for open-source tool that I can run offline
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I used Microsoft Excel for years because it was the spreadsheet tool I already knew. But over time, I started wondering if I really needed to keep using it. I didn't want to spend time learning a completely different spreadsheet app either. I just wanted something practical that I could install, open, and use without adding another dependency to my setup. I tried a few alternatives, including Google Sheets, but eventually found myself sticking with LibreOffice Calc. It wasn't a dramatic switch or a decision I made overnight. It simply turned out to be the spreadsheet app that made the most sense for me.

LibreOffice Calc became my go-to spreadsheet

Familiar enough to feel effortless

LibreCalc felt familiar enough that I could start using it without having to relearn how spreadsheets work. Rows, columns, formulas, sheets, formatting, and the usual spreadsheet tools were all where I expected them to be. I could open an existing workbook, make changes, and get on with what I needed to do without spending time figuring out a completely different approach.

I also liked that Calc didn't try to make me change the way I think about spreadsheets. I wasn't looking for something radically different from Excel. I simply wanted a capable replacement that didn't make me feel like I was giving up the spreadsheet features I had become accustomed to. After using it for a while, Calc stopped feeling like an alternative I was testing and became the spreadsheet application I naturally reached for.

It doesn't care whether I'm online

Offline access is built right in

One thing I really like about Calc is that it doesn't care if I'm online or not. I can open it and start working without first checking my internet connection. I've used it when my internet was down and while traveling, and it never really mattered. Calc just opened and worked as usual.

I don't have to wait for anything to load or worry about losing access because my connection isn't working. If I have a spreadsheet on my computer, I can open it whenever I need it. This comes in handy for those small tasks where I just need to check a number, change something, or update a few cells. It feels unnecessary to depend on an internet connection for something that simple.

LibreOffice proved that paying for Microsoft 365 was my biggest mistake

Why LibreOffice is a productivity powerhouse, not a downgrade.

By  Yash Patel

Smoothly handles my spreadsheet workflow

It has more than enough for me

Calc handles pretty much everything I normally expect from a spreadsheet. I don't use spreadsheets for anything too complicated, but I still want the basic tools to be there when I need them. I regularly use formulas for calculations, and Calc supports the common functions I rely on. Sorting and filtering are also straightforward when I'm dealing with a longer list of data. I can quickly find what I need without doing much extra work.

I also make use of charts when I want to turn a table of numbers into something easier to understand. Pivot tables are useful when I need to group or summarize a larger set of data, while conditional formatting helps me highlight important values. Another thing I like is the support for different file formats. I can work with Excel files, CSV files, and Calc's own spreadsheet format without having to convert everything beforehand. Calc also includes tools like data validation, named ranges, multiple sheet management, and basic macro support. I don't use all of these every day, but it's good knowing they're available when a spreadsheet gets a little more involved.

Looks a bit old-school

Open-source benefits overpower the interface

Calc isn't the prettiest spreadsheet app I've used. The interface definitely feels a little old-school, especially compared with newer apps that put more effort into modern design. Some menus and buttons look like they came from an older generation of desktop software.

At first, that bothered me a little. I was used to cleaner interfaces, so Calc took some getting used to. But after spending more time with it, I stopped noticing it as much. What helped was remembering why I chose Calc in the first place. It's open-source, free to use, and I don't have to pay for a subscription just to keep using it. I can also install it on different computers without worrying about another license. Those things matter more to me than having a perfectly polished interface. I'd rather put up with a slightly dated look and have software that gives me that freedom.

This one free open-source tool replaced three paid apps I'd used for years

I thought free office suites always came with compromises, but this open-source tool proved I was completely wrong.

item.title: Half your case fans are plugged into headers your motherboard can't actually control
item.itunes:title: Half your case fans are plugged into headers your motherboard can't actually control
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I built my first PC well over a decade ago, I treated every fan header on my motherboard more or less the same. Rookie mistake, I know, but as long as the connector fit and the fan started spinning, I assumed everything was fine. And to be fair, things were a little more confusing back then, since my old Z77 motherboard had both 3-pin and 4-pin fan headers. Nowadays, though, pretty much every fan header you'll find on a motherboard is 4-pin, so you might think there's not much you can get wrong.

Except it's not quite that simple. A 4-pin header doesn't always mean your motherboard has proper control over whatever fan you connect to it. And that matters more when we're talking about case fans, since you could still be using 3-pin DC fans that plug into those headers just fine. There's also a good chance you have multiple fans connected to the same header through a splitter or fan hub, which introduces another limitation that isn't immediately obvious. So if you've never paid attention to how they're connected, now would be a good time to take another look.

4 ways PC builders mess up their case fan configuration

Fan configuration is one of the easiest things to overlook, but thankfully, it's also one of the easiest things to fix.

5
By  Ty Sherback

PWM mode can't control your 3-pin case fans

They'll just run at full speed regardless of your fan curve

The problem with plugging a 3-pin fan into a 4-pin header is that the extra pin is there for the PWM signal that controls the fan's speed. A 3-pin fan doesn't have that fourth pin, so if you have your motherboard's fan header set to PWM mode, it has no way of receiving the signal telling it to speed up or slow down. The fan will still get 12V through the power pin and spin normally, which is exactly why this is so easy to overlook. So even if you set a fan curve in your BIOS, the fan will just keep running at full speed.

That's where DC mode comes in, though. Instead of keeping the fan at 12V, DC mode controls its speed by varying the voltage supplied to it. This means your 3-pin fan can still follow a temperature-based fan curve just like you'd expect, but with less precise control at lower speeds. Even though most motherboards have an Auto mode that can detect whether you've connected a 3-pin or 4-pin fan, it's not universal. Depending on your motherboard, some headers may default to Auto, whereas others may default to PWM mode. So it's worth making sure your case fans are connected to the appropriate headers and that each one is using the right mode in your BIOS.

Fan splitters take away individual fan control

Every fan connected to the same header follows the same curve

If your case is airflow-oriented and loaded with fans like mine, there's a good chance you're using a fan splitter to connect them all. After all, even higher-end motherboards only give you so many chassis fan headers, so you may not have enough to connect every fan individually. Sure, daisy-chaining makes things a lot easier if your fans support it, but that doesn't give you any more control. Whether you have three fans connected through a splitter or daisy-chained together, they're still ultimately connected to the same header.

What this means is that they all receive the same control signal and follow the same fan curve, so you can't really adjust their speed individually. Of course, that's not a problem if those fans are all doing the same job. I have three intake fans at the front of my case and another three at the top, and it makes sense to treat each set as its own group. But you shouldn't randomly connect three fans to the same header just because it's more convenient. If you're using a splitter or a hub, group fans based on what they're actually doing in your case, whether they're being used for intake, exhaust, or a radiator.

Motherboards do make this foolproof for the most part

Yes, Auto mode does most of the work for you, but you shouldn't blindly trust it

Motherboards nowadays make it pretty difficult to get any of this completely wrong. As I mentioned earlier, Auto mode can switch between DC and PWM depending on whether you've connected a 3-pin or 4-pin case fan. So even if you've never opened the fan control section in your BIOS, your case fans are probably already working exactly as they should. This actually helps beginners who don't understand everything that's happening behind the scenes.

But I still wouldn't assume your motherboard has everything configured correctly. Auto-detection may not be available on every fan header, depending on the motherboard you have, so some headers could be set to PWM or DC by default. For instance, the pump header on the MSI X870 boards defaults to PWM mode, which is exactly what you want for AIO pumps, but if you accidentally plugged a 3-pin case fan into it, it'll just run at full speed. And even when Auto mode works perfectly, you're not going to get individual fan control if you've used a splitter.

Your case fans may be fine, but it's still worth checking

I didn't write this article to point out that everyone's making some mistake with their case fans. I truly believe most of our readers already know their way around a PC. But fan control is also one of those things that's easy to miss because your fans can spin just fine even when everything isn't configured correctly. You may not realize something's wrong until you mess with the fan curves. So it doesn't hurt to revisit your BIOS to make sure each header is using the right mode and that you've grouped your fans in a way that actually makes sense.
